newsitem.title: CHINA: China's finance markets undergo fundamental change.
newsitem.headline: China's finance markets undergo fundamental change.

text.p: China's financial markets are undergoing fundamental changes in the face of concerted efforts by Beijing to force both investors and institutions to stick to the rules, analysts said on Thursday.
With the shadow of economic czar Vice Premier Zhu Rongji looming large over them, the markets were for the first time beginning to take the regulations to heart, they said.
Analysts said the markets would undoubtedly benefit in the long run.
Since early May, the securities authorities have issued a string of edicts and punishments which have sent the markets reeling and speculators running for cover.

The bull run which pushed stock prices up by more than 50 percent in the first few months of this year has been stopped dead in its tracks, and trading volumes have dropped significantly in line with Zhu's desire to cut volatility.
"You can no longer talk of China having bull markets or bear markets, there is only Zhu's market," said an analyst at one brokerage in Shanghai.

Banks and state enterprises, once the mainstays of share trading, are withdrawing their funds from the stock markets, and brokerages are under notice to clean up trading to prevent unauthorised funds from leaking into stocks.
State banks have also been banned from trading on the state debt repurchase and spot markets.

"The recent crackdown has bridged the gap between the rules and practice to a great extent," said one local banker. "Before the crackdown, the rules were largely ignored and many traders believed the markets could not operate without irregularities."
Analysts said the most important effect of the crackdown measures so far was to stop bank funds flowing through the brokerages into the stock markets.
"There are always loopholes, but it appears they are being quite successful in stopping the flow of bank and state enterprise funds into stocks," said an analyst at a Chinese brokerage.
"They want to make the stock markets a place largely for retail investors, while bank and enterprise funds are used to expand production," the analyst said.

Analysts said the withdrawal of institutional funds from the stock markets would sharply reduce speculation, while the shift of bank money to the standardised interbank market would boost the development of the financial system.

"The crackdown is helping to make the financial markets more of an investment vehicle and less of a casino," said an executive with a Chinese brokerage said. "This will make them more attractive to both domestic and foreign investors."
As part of the crackdown, key listed firms including the Shenzhen Development Bank Co and the nation's top brokerage, Shenyin and Wanguo Securities, were punished for irregularities.
But analysts said China's markets, founded only in the early 1990s, still had a long way to go to reach internationally accepted levels of maturity.
"Fundamental changes are occurring in our financial markets but we cannot expect them to mature for several more years at least," a banker said.
